title: Test 5 — Redundancy, Monitoring & Racks
blurb: Concurrent maintainability, tiers and N levels, BMS/EPMS, rounds and trending, busways, containment and rackdown response.

questions.q: Why is redundancy built into a data center, according to Amazon's own material?
choices: Solely to survive unplanned equipment failures
To withstand an unplanned event and keep power to the critical load, AND to allow maintenance personnel to perform required PM on equipment
To reduce PUE by sharing load across more units
To meet utility interconnection requirements
questions.why: Both halves matter. Without redundancy there is no safe window to do PM at all — that's the link between redundancy and concurrent maintainability.

questions.q: A facility has three chillers and needs two to carry design load. What is this?
choices: 2N
questions.why: N is the capacity required (two chillers). One spare beyond that is N+1.

questions.q: In a 2N electrical design, what does taking one entire distribution path out of service do to the load?
choices: Drops half the load until the path is restored
Nothing — the load is fully duplicated and the other path carries it
Forces a transfer to the generator
Requires the UPS to run on battery for the duration
questions.why: 2N is a fully duplicated system. That's what makes whole-path maintenance possible.

questions.q: Concurrent maintainability and fault tolerance differ how?
choices: Concurrent maintainability covers planned work; fault tolerance covers surviving an unplanned failure
Concurrent maintainability applies to mechanical only; fault tolerance to electrical only
They are two terms for the same design property
Fault tolerance is a subset of concurrent maintainability
questions.why: Planned versus unplanned is the whole distinction. Both come from redundancy, but they answer different questions.

questions.q: Why does a mechanical technician specifically care about concurrent maintainability?
choices: It determines the chilled water setpoint
It's what allows a chiller, pump or CRAH to be taken out of service for work while the critical load keeps running
It sets the PM interval for rotating equipment
It governs which loop is primary during free cooling
questions.why: No redundancy means no safe window for PM — you'd have to choose between maintenance and uptime.

questions.q: You're assigned to PM a UPS in an N+1 configuration and one of the other units is already down for repair. What has changed?
choices: Nothing — N+1 means one unit can always be removed
You've lost your redundancy margin; taking a second unit out puts the critical load at N or below, so this needs escalation before you proceed
You should proceed but shorten the PM
You should transfer the load to generator first
questions.why: Knowing your current redundancy state before starting work is the practical form of this concept. Interviewers probe exactly this.

questions.q: What is a single point of failure?
choices: Any component that has failed more than once
Any component whose failure drops the critical load
The component with the longest lead time for replacement
The first device to trip in a coordinated scheme
questions.why: Data centers are designed to eliminate them so no single failure takes down customers.

questions.q: Amazon's target uptime is stated as:
choices: 99.9% or better
99.99% or better
99.9999% or better
questions.why: Roughly 30 seconds of downtime per year. Quote the figure — it's stated directly in the prep material.

questions.q: Which system would you use to check chiller status, CRAH valve position and space humidity?
choices: EPMS
BMS
The rPDU controller
The fire alarm control panel
questions.why: BMS = Building Management System, the mechanical side: chillers, CRAHs, pumps, temperature, humidity, airflow, dampers, alarms.

questions.q: Which system would you use to check breaker status, load on a feeder and power quality?
choices: BMS
EPMS
SCADA
The UPS local display only
questions.why: EPMS = Electrical Power (or Plant) Monitoring System: metering, breaker status, power quality, load, alarms.

questions.q: What are the inputs to these monitoring systems?
choices: Operator log entries only
Meters, devices and communications networks
The PM work order system
Utility SCADA feeds
questions.why: The prep material names these explicitly — understanding the inputs is listed as part of the responsibility, not just reading the screen.

questions.q: The BMS goes offline. What is the operational consequence you should name first?
choices: Cooling equipment stops running
You lose visibility and automated alarming, so detection now depends on physical rounds and local panels — increase round frequency and escalate
PUE reporting is interrupted
The EPMS takes over BMS points automatically
questions.why: Equipment generally keeps running on local control. The loss is visibility, which is why knowing what actions to take on a monitoring system failure is a stated expectation.

questions.q: Generating reports and trends from the BMS/EPMS is expected of an EOT because:
choices: It is required for the annual impairment filing
Trends show a condition developing over time — a bearing slowly heating, an approach temperature creeping up — which a spot reading can't
Reports are needed to close out work orders
It replaces the need for rounds
questions.why: AWS is a data driven company. Analyzing metrics like PUE and WUE is called out as an EOT expectation.

questions.q: What is the value of physical rounds and log taking when you already have a BMS and EPMS?
choices: Rounds satisfy an insurance requirement
They catch what sensors miss — leaks, noises, smells, corrosion, loose connections, heat
They are how monitoring points get calibrated
They provide a manual backup log if the BMS database is lost
questions.why: Instrumentation doesn't see everything. Visual monitoring in the form of rounds and log taking is listed as an additional responsibility.

questions.q: During rounds you notice a faint burning smell near a switchboard but every reading is normal. What do you do?
choices: Log it and continue the round — the data doesn't support a fault
Stop, investigate, and escalate — a smell with normal readings is exactly the case where instrumentation is blind, and loose terminations are the classic cause of electrical fires
Reset the affected meter and re-read
Wait for the next round to see if it persists
questions.why: This also lines up with thermal imaging as a preventive tool for finding hot spots from loose or degrading connections.

questions.q: A meter reading and your physical observation disagree. Correct approach?
choices: Trust the calibrated instrument over subjective observation
Investigate rather than assume the instrument is right, and verify with a second method
Log the discrepancy for the next shift
Replace the sensor and re-read
questions.why: A faulty sensor and a real fault look identical on a screen. Dive Deep explicitly names being skeptical when metrics and anecdote differ.

questions.q: What is an EOT's responsibility at the rack level?
choices: Installing and cabling servers into racks
Not rack-level tasks, but ensuring racks are properly powered up and cooled, and current is properly balanced across sources
Managing rack capacity planning for customers
Configuring rPDU network settings
questions.why: The prep material is explicit: engineers aren't responsible for rack level tasks, but they are responsible for power, cooling and balance.

questions.q: Why must current be balanced across both sources feeding a rack?
choices: To keep the neutral from carrying excessive current
To prevent overloading a single source — if the heavily loaded side fails, the other may not be able to carry the whole load
To reduce harmonic distortion at the PDU
Balance is a metering convention, not an operational concern
questions.why: Preventing overload of a single source is the exact phrasing in the material. It's what makes dual-feed redundancy real rather than nominal.

questions.q: Busway and tap box, in order:
choices: Overhead bus-bar distribution running above the rows; the point where a circuit is tapped off it to feed a rack without cutting conductors
A cable tray system; a junction box for splices
The floor-level distribution unit; its output breaker panel
The in-rack power strip; its input connector
questions.why: The tap box is what makes adding or moving rack feeds a plug-in operation instead of an electrical modification.

questions.q: What is an rPDU?
choices: A redundant PDU paired with the primary floor unit
The power strip in the rack that servers plug into
A rack-mounted transfer switch
A remote PDU controller on the building network
questions.why: The PDU is the floor-level unit doing transformation and branch distribution; the rPDU is the in-rack strip.

questions.q: Hot aisle / cold aisle containment exists to:
choices: Reduce noise exposure in the data hall
Keep cold supply air and hot exhaust air physically separated so the two streams don't mix
Allow individual racks to be isolated during maintenance
Create positive pressure against outside contaminants
questions.why: Mixing means you cool air that's already cold, waste energy, raise PUE, and can leave server intakes hot even when room average looks fine.

questions.q: EOTs are expected to be first responders to what rack-level event?
choices: Server hardware failures
Rackdown events
Network switch outages
Cable management violations
questions.why: Named directly in the prep material. It's the one rack-level thing that's squarely an EOT responsibility.

questions.q: A rack has gone down. What is the first thing to establish?
choices: Which customer workloads were affected
Whether it lost one source or both — one source down means the rack should have stayed up on the other, which points to a balance, breaker or cord problem rather than an upstream failure
Whether the room temperature is within ASHRAE limits
Whether the rPDU firmware is current
questions.why: Dual-fed racks shouldn't drop on a single source loss. If it did, the redundancy was not actually there — often because load wasn't balanced.

questions.q: You find a rack drawing 80% of its load from the A source and 20% from B. Why does that matter even though nothing has failed?
choices: It causes premature rPDU wear
If A fails, B has to pick up the full load and may trip — the rack looks redundant but isn't
It skews PUE calculations
It creates a phase imbalance at the transformer
questions.why: Latent single point of failure. This is a strong example to bring into an Ownership or Dive Deep story.

questions.q: PUE is:
choices: IT equipment power ÷ total facility power
Total facility power ÷ IT equipment power
Cooling power ÷ total facility power
Total facility power ÷ design capacity
questions.why: 1.0 is theoretically perfect; cooling is the main driver upward. AWS expects EOTs to analyze it as a key metric.

questions.q: WUE measures:
choices: Water consumed per unit of IT energy
Water discharged as blowdown per year
Cooling tower efficiency versus wet bulb
Makeup water as a percentage of evaporation
questions.why: Evaporative cooling lowers PUE but raises WUE. Naming that as a real tradeoff rather than a free win is what scores.

questions.q: Which cooling modes does the prep material name, and what governs which one is used?
choices: Free cooling, recirculation and mechanical cooling — selected by outside conditions and load, with direct effects on PUE and WUE
Chilled water and DX only, selected by building design
Economizer and emergency, selected by the BMS schedule
Evaporative and conductive, selected by season
questions.why: Understanding when each mode is used and how it affects PUE and WUE is called out as an explicit expectation.

questions.q: The plant switches from free cooling to mechanical cooling. What has most likely happened?
choices: Chilled water flow dropped below minimum
Outside conditions — wet bulb or dry bulb — rose past the point where the tower or outside air can carry the load alone
A CRAH went into maintenance mode
WUE exceeded its target
questions.why: Free cooling depends on ambient. That's why facilities get built in cool, dry climates — more free cooling hours, lower PUE.

questions.q: The EPMS shows a breaker open that your rounds sheet says should be closed. First move?
choices: Close the breaker to restore the normal configuration
Verify the actual physical position and find out why before changing anything — the alarm may be a status point fault or a real trip with a cause
Log it and report at shift change
Reset the EPMS point
questions.why: Never operate a critical breaker to 'fix' a display. Verify state, understand cause, follow the procedure.

questions.q: Why does knowing your building's specific tier and N level matter during an emergency, not just during PM?
choices: It determines which vendor to call
It tells you how much margin you have left — what you can lose next without dropping load — which drives how urgently you escalate
It sets the alarm thresholds in the BMS
It determines the order of load shed
questions.why: Redundancy state is situational awareness. "We're down to N" is a different emergency than "we're still at N+1."
